solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Most well-upholstered bath cap that one wears (8)

indicators.note: one wears clothes around the body, so BEST wears I by wrapping round it

blocks.note: to cap is to top or beat, i.e. to best
I = one, as the Roman numeral

explanation.surface: A bathroom scene: someone plump pulling on a bath cap.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cap' looks like a noun going with 'bath'; it is the verb, to outdo.
explanation.definitionFit: Well-upholstered is a jokey idiom for plump, as if the body were a padded armchair, and tubby is the everyday word for plump.

clue.text: Swollen stomach I feed without restraint (8)

indicators.note: letters with no restraint on them are free to wander, so I FEED comes out in a new order

blocks.note: tum is an informal word for the stomach

explanation.surface: Someone who eats without limits ends up with a bloated belly.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface ties 'swollen' to 'stomach', so the definition seems to be the whole phrase; it is only the first word.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym from medical language: tissue that has become tumid, from the Latin for swelling, is tumefied.

clue.text: Corporate mover and shaker? (5,6)

blocks.note: reads as belonging to a company; the setter means belonging to the body, via 'corporation', a jokey old word for a paunch
reads as an influential executive; the setter means someone who literally moves and shakes

explanation.surface: A business profile of a dynamic figure in the corporate world.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark warns that the business jargon is to be taken literally: a mover and shaker of the midriff.
explanation.definitionFit: A performer who shimmies the stomach is a mover and shaker of the body's 'corporation'.

clue.text: When to cut awfully nice red rose (9)

indicators.note: a blade cuts into what it slices, so AS goes into the middle of the other letters
something done awfully is botched, so NICE RED comes out jumbled

explanation.surface: A gardener deciding when to prune an unattractive red rose.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rose' reads as the flower in a gardening scene; it is the past tense of rise.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym once 'rose' is read as a verb: whatever rose went up in amount or level.

clue.text: Smart son idiot upset heading for graduation (5)

indicators.note: to upset is to knock over, and in a down entry a word knocked over reads bottom to top
the heading of a word is what stands at its top, its first letter

explanation.surface: A clever son whose idiot sibling is upset about going off to graduate.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Smart' looks like an adjective describing the son; it is the verb, to hurt sharply.
explanation.definitionFit: Read as a verb, smart means to feel a sharp burning pain, which is what a wound or a nettle does to you.

clue.text: Parents in need of bit of mollifying rest (6)

indicators.note: someone in need of a thing lacks it, so MOTHERS lacks the letter that follows
the smallest bit of a word is a single letter, and the one taken is its first

blocks.note: first letter of mollifying, taken away

explanation.surface: Weary parents who need soothing and some rest.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface makes 'rest' sound like sleep; it means the remainder, as in 'the rest of them'.
explanation.definitionFit: Taking 'rest' as the remainder, the people left over once some are counted are the others.

clue.text: Rotten to run into extremely tedious posh peeps (5)

indicators.note: a car that runs into a wall ends up in it, so OFF ends up between the other letters
a word's extremes are its two ends, so tedious gives just T and S

blocks.note: food that has gone off is rotten

explanation.surface: A sneer at dull, rotten upper-class people.
explanation.walkthrough: A toff is British slang for an upper-class person; 'peeps' is slang for people.
explanation.definitionFit: A regional use: in British slang a toff is a smartly dressed, well-off person, exactly what posh people are.

clue.text: I try to follow edicts… at first (3)

indicators.note: what follows comes after, so in a down entry GO sits below E
what a word shows at first is its opening letter

blocks.note: have a go = have a try

explanation.surface: Someone vowing to obey rules, at least initially.
explanation.walkthrough: 'I' seems to be the speaker of the sentence; it is the definition, the self.
explanation.definitionFit: Ego is Latin for I, and in psychology the ego is the conscious self that says I.

clue.text: One picked up by George Harrison? (5)

definitions.text: One picked up by George Harrison?

blocks.note: reads as something lifted or collected; the setter means something learned, and also something plucked
the Beatle who studied Indian music in the 1960s and played it on Beatles records

explanation.surface: Something the Beatle George Harrison lifted or collected.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Picked up' works twice: Harrison picked up (learned) the instrument in the 1960s, and its strings are picked, i.e. plucked.
explanation.definitionFit: George Harrison famously took lessons from Ravi Shankar and played the Indian stringed instrument on 'Norwegian Wood'.

clue.text: Imprisoned nurse inside abstained from food (8)

indicators.note: the nurse is put inside, like a prisoner, so EN sits within FASTED

blocks.note: to fast is to go without food

explanation.surface: A jailed nurse who went on hunger strike.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Imprisoned' and 'abstained from food' paint a hunger strike; the first is the definition, the second the outer shell.
explanation.definitionFit: A loose synonym: something fastened is held fast and cannot get away, as a prisoner is.

clue.text: Prophet from a church in African state (7)

indicators.note: the plain preposition: A CH is placed in the state, i.e. inside MALI

explanation.surface: A prophet who comes from a church in Africa.
explanation.walkthrough: The capital P hides nothing here; the surface simply borrows the biblical flavour.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by example: Malachi is the last of the minor prophets, with the final book of the Old Testament named after him.

clue.text: Deliberately offensive act in a show on radio (7)

indicators.note: on the radio words are heard, not seen, so only the sound counts

blocks.note: a front is a show, as in 'putting on a front'

explanation.surface: A radio show containing a deliberately offensive act.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Show' looks like a programme on the radio; it means a pretence, a front.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: an affront is an insult delivered on purpose, from the old sense of striking someone in the face.

clue.text: One boxes whey gift up with muscleman essentially (9)

indicators.note: letters that are stirred up are in a mess, so WHEY GIFT comes out in a new order
the essence of something is at its heart, so muscleman gives its central letter

blocks.note: middle letter of muscleman, added to the fodder

explanation.surface: A gym scene: whey protein handed to a muscleman as a present.
explanation.walkthrough: 'One boxes' looks like someone packing things; it is someone who boxes, a boxer.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by example: a flyweight is a boxer in the lightest standard weight class, so one who boxes.

clue.text: Plain and dull as all teetotallers are? (5)

blocks.note: the sense used of muted colours or a restrained suit
people who never drink are never drunk

explanation.surface: A dig at teetotallers as boring people.
explanation.walkthrough: The joke is that both senses seem to describe the same dull non-drinker.
explanation.definitionFit: Sober covers both senses: restrained and colourless in style, and not affected by alcohol.

clue.text: Scrappy green belt I hooked round back of heel (11)

indicators.note: something hooked is bent out of shape, so GREEN BELT I is twisted into a new order
the rearranged letters go round the next letter, holding it inside
the back of a word is its end, so heel gives its last letter

blocks.note: last letter of heel, placed inside

explanation.surface: A martial-arts fighter with a green belt landing a hooked kick round the back of an opponent's heel.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Scrappy' seems to mean untidy; it means keen to scrap, i.e. fight, which fits the fighting surface.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: a scrap is a fight, so a scrappy person is combative and aggressive.

clue.text: Chopper to be reviewed by Sunday after mass tests (5)

indicators.note: reviewed read as re-viewed, viewed again from the other end, so the word turns round
S comes after M, so M is put down first

explanation.surface: A tool to be reviewed on Sunday once the church service and some trials are over.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Mass' suggests the Sunday church service; here it is the physics symbol m.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: examinations are formal tests of knowledge.

clue.text: Privates stealing explosive (8)

indicators.note: an explosion blows things apart and scatters them, so STEALING lands in a new order

explanation.surface: Army privates caught stealing explosives.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Privates' looks like soldiers, which the explosive fits; it is the euphemism for the sexual organs.
explanation.definitionFit: An idiom: 'private parts', shortened to privates, is the polite euphemism for the sexual organs.

clue.text: Flappers seen with unhealthy-looking convicts (8)

blocks.note: old lag is British slang for a convict

explanation.surface: Nineteen-twenties flapper girls keeping company with pasty jailbirds.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Flappers' suggests the 1920s party girls; here it is things that flap their wings. Greylags are grey wild geese.
explanation.definitionFit: A cryptic sense by example: greylag geese are big birds that flap their wings, so are flappers.

clue.text: They have a tinkle in large tins after surgery (9)

indicators.note: surgery cuts a body open and rearranges its parts, so LARGE TINS comes out in a new order

explanation.surface: Hospital patients relieving themselves in big tins after an operation.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tinkle' suggests urinating, which the surgery scene encourages; here it is the tinkling sound of the percussion instrument.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by description: the orchestral triangle, a bent steel bar struck with a beater, gives a bright tinkle.

clue.text: Bag up sofa without using last of adhesive tape (8)

indicators.note: in a down entry, going up means reading from bottom to top, so SAC turns round
doing without something means leaving it out, so SETTEE drops a letter
the last of a word is its final letter

blocks.note: last letter of adhesive, one E dropped from SETTEE

explanation.surface: Instructions for bagging up a sofa without using sticky tape.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Adhesive tape' reads as one thing, sticky tape; 'tape' alone is the definition, the audio kind.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: a cassette is magnetic recording tape wound inside a small plastic case.

clue.text: Tripper did ache badly after accident at front (8)

indicators.note: something done badly is done wrong, so DID ACHE comes out in the wrong order
the jumbled letters come after the A, so the A is written first
what stands at the front of a word is its first letter

explanation.surface: A day-tripper nursing aches after a mishap.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tripper' looks like a tourist or someone who stumbles; here it is someone who takes LSD trips.
explanation.definitionFit: Slang: acid is LSD and a head is a habitual user, and an LSD experience is called a trip.

clue.text: Business located in Iowa holiday spot (5)

indicators.note: a business located in a place sits inside it, so BIZ goes inside IA

blocks.note: IA is the postal code for Iowa
biz is slang for business, as in showbiz

explanation.surface: A company based in an Iowa vacation resort.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface places the holiday spot in Iowa; the answer is a Spanish island.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by example: Ibiza, in the Balearics, is a Mediterranean island famous for beach holidays and clubbing.

clue.text: Knaves smuggling rupees for knaves? (5)

indicators.note: smugglers carry goods hidden inside, so CADS hold R within them

blocks.note: cads are knaves, dishonourable men; the setter repeats the word on purpose

explanation.surface: Rogues smuggling Indian money in exchange for more rogues.
explanation.walkthrough: The word 'knaves' appears twice with different jobs: first the rogues, then, with the question mark, the jacks in a pack.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by example: the knave is the old name for the jack, one of the court cards in a pack.

clue.text: Go after husband during legal proceedings (5)

indicators.note: what happens during something falls within its span, so H falls within CASE

explanation.surface: Pursuing a husband while divorce proceedings are under way.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface reads 'go after husband' as one phrase; 'Go after' is the definition and husband is the letter H.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: to chase someone is to run after them in pursuit.

clue.text: Polish hotel admitted to error with pride ultimately (5)

indicators.note: someone admitted to a place is let in, so H is let into SIN
E goes along with the rest, tagged on after it
what comes ultimately comes last, so pride gives its final letter

blocks.note: a sin is a moral error
H = hotel in the NATO phonetic alphabet

explanation.surface: A Polish hotelier admitting a proud mistake.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Polish' is capitalised as the nationality to fit the hotel; it is the verb, to polish.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: to polish shoes or brass is to rub them until they gleam.

clue.text: Reason old queen enters loos to get perfumes? (9)

indicators.note: someone who enters a room ends up inside it, so END ER end up inside LAVS

blocks.note: an end is a purpose or reason

explanation.surface: A former queen visiting the toilets to freshen up with scent.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark flags a definition by example: lavender is one kind of perfume.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by example: lavender water, distilled from the fragrant plant, is a classic scent.

clue.text: One collared by police unit mostly on a river (5)

indicators.note: most but not all of a word is kept, so VICE loses its last letter
in a down entry, one thing on another sits above it, so VIC comes before A R

blocks.note: the vice squad, minus its last letter

explanation.surface: A suspect nabbed by a river police patrol.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Collared' suggests arrested, fitting the police; here it means wearing a clerical, or dog, collar.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by description: a vicar is a parish priest, who wears the white clerical collar.

clue.text: Thinking on drop of alcohol can be funny (7)

indicators.note: one thing placed on another follows it in an across entry, so MUSING is written after A
a drop is the smallest amount, so alcohol gives only its first letter

explanation.surface: A remark that thoughts become comic after a drink.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Drop of alcohol' reads as a small drink; it is just the one letter at the front.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: something amusing makes you laugh or smile.

clue.text: Do drugs you possess deteriorate in the end? (3)

indicators.note: the end of a word is its final letter, taken from both possess and deteriorate

blocks.note: U = you, as in text messages
last letters of possess and deteriorate

explanation.surface: A warning question: will taking drugs make you worse eventually?
explanation.walkthrough: 'In the end' sounds like 'eventually' in the surface; it tells you to take final letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Slang: a drug user who 'uses' is taking drugs habitually.

clue.text: Gather together some protocol lectures (7)

indicators.note: only some of the letters of protocol lectures are used, a run inside them

explanation.surface: Assembling a group for talks on diplomatic etiquette.
explanation.walkthrough: The answer straddles the gap between the two words, which is what makes it hard to see.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: to collect things or people is to bring them into one place.

clue.text: Sports team possibly drawn by The Spanish (6)

indicators.note: by means next to, so EVEN stands beside EL, after it

explanation.surface: A team that drew its match against Spain.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Possibly' is there because only some sports, such as cricket and football, field teams of that size.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by example: a cricket or football side has that many players and is called by the number.

clue.text: Earl put on outfit with this on occasion? (5,3)

definitions.text: Earl put on outfit with this on occasion?

indicators.note: one thing put on another is added to it, so E is tacked onto the end
only now and then, so this gives every other letter, T and I

blocks.note: first and third letters of this

explanation.surface: An aristocrat dressing up for a formal event.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue is also the definition: this is what an earl might put on with evening dress on a formal occasion.
explanation.definitionFit: Read straight, the clue describes formal neckwear: a bow tie worn with evening dress on special occasions.
